stages.title: Types of literature
stages.hook: A library has shelves for stories, facts, poems and plays. How would you sort a thousand books?
explain: Literature is writing that people value for its story, ideas or beauty. We sort it into types. Fiction is made up, such as a fairy tale or an adventure. Nonfiction tells about real things, such as a biography or a book about volcanoes.

Fiction has genres, which are families of stories with shared features: fantasy has magic, mystery has a puzzle to solve, adventure has danger and travel, and science fiction imagines science and the future.
Not all literature was written down. Oral literature is spoken or sung and passed on from person to person. Folktales, riddles and songs belong here.

example.q: Sort the books: a book on how bees make honey, a story about a talking fox, a life of a famous inventor.
steps: Ask: is it real or made up?
Bees and inventor are real, so nonfiction.
The talking fox is made up, so fiction.
example.a: Fiction: the fox story. Nonfiction: the bees and the inventor.

analogies.home: Cookery books are nonfiction, bedtime tales are fiction.
analogies.city: A library has a fiction shelf and a nonfiction shelf.
analogies.farm: A farmer's guide to crops is nonfiction; a tale of a clever hen is fiction.
analogies.music: A song can tell a story just like a book.

stages.mnemonic: FIct = made up, FAct = real: fiction invents, fact-books tell what is.
terms: Writing about made-up people and events.
Writing about real facts and true events.
A family of writing with shared features, such as mystery.
Stories, songs and poems passed on by speaking.

misc.wrong: Literature only means books with printed pages.
misc.right: Literature includes spoken stories, songs and plays as well as written works.

stages.limits: Some works mix real settings with made-up characters (historical fiction), so the line is not always sharp.

trip.prompt: Find three genres and one famous example of each.

questions.q: Which is nonfiction?
o: A book about how volcanoes erupt
A tale of a dragon who bakes bread
A story of a talking tree
A poem about an imaginary moon city

questions.q: A story has a wizard and a magic wand. Which genre is it?
What is a genre?
o: A kind of writing with shared features
A set of rules for how to spell and print the words in any book
The name of the person who wrote it

questions.q: A tale has a detective hunting for who took a lost necklace. Which genre?
questions.why: A puzzle to solve is the key of mystery.

questions.q: Which is an example of oral literature?
o: A tale told round a fire and never written
A printed dictionary kept on a library shelf
questions.why: Oral literature is spoken and passed on.

questions.q: A book follows a girl on a spaceship visiting new planets. Which genre?
o: A biography of a real person
questions.why: Imagined science and travel suggest science fiction.

questions.q: Match each book to its type.
pairs: The life of a real explorer
questions.why: Real lives are nonfiction; folktales are fiction; sung riddles are oral.

questions.q: Why do libraries separate fiction from nonfiction?
o: Readers can find what kind of book they need
Fiction is always better than nonfiction books

questions.q: Explain the difference between fiction and nonfiction in your own words.
questions.model: Fiction is made up by the author, while nonfiction tells about real facts and true events.
questions.why: Both ideas are needed: fiction is invented, nonfiction is real.

questions.q: A book tells of a real war but follows invented characters. What is it?
o: A diary of a real person
questions.why: Real setting plus invented people is historical fiction.

panel.q: Why can a folktale be called literature even if never written?
o: Its words are valued and shared, even when spoken
Only things that are written down can count as literature
Because it has pictures in it

panel.q: A book is called a memoir, written by a person about their life. Is it fiction or nonfiction, and why?
panel.model: Nonfiction, because it tells real events from the writer's life, as they remember them.
panel.why: A memoir is about real experiences.

panel.q: Why might two readers disagree whether a legend is fiction or fact?
o: Some legends mix real events with imagined ones
Legends are always completely true, so there is no argument
panel.why: Legends can blend history and imagination.

teach.model: Literature is writing and spoken art that people value. Fiction is made up and nonfiction is real. Genres are families like fantasy and mystery. Oral literature is spoken, such as folktales.

stages.title: Prose, poetry and drama
stages.hook: A joke can be told in a sentence, a rhyme or a little play. How do the three forms feel different?
explain: The three main forms are prose, poetry and drama. Prose is ordinary writing in sentences and paragraphs, as in novels and short stories.
Poetry is arranged in lines, often with rhythm, rhyme and strong pictures in few words. Lines are grouped in stanzas.
Drama is written to be performed. A script has characters' speech (dialogue) and stage directions that tell actors what to do. A play is divided into acts and scenes.

example.q: Name the form: "KING: Who goes there? (He steps back.)"
steps: Speaker's name followed by speech: dialogue.
Words in brackets tell what to do: a stage direction.
These are signs of a script.

analogies.home: A family dinner is prose, a lullaby is poetry, a living-room puppet show is drama.
analogies.city: A newspaper uses prose, a poster may use a poem, a street show is drama.
analogies.music: Poetry is close to song lyrics.
analogies.sea: A ship's log is prose, a sea shanty is poetry.

stages.mnemonic: Prose is a flat road, poetry a dance in lines, drama a stage with actors.
terms: Writing in ordinary sentences and paragraphs.
A group of lines in a poem.
A note in a script about action or setting.

misc.right: Many poems do not rhyme; rhythm, lines and images matter too.

trip.prompt: Find the parts of a play and what actors do with a script.

questions.q: Which form is written to be acted?
What is a stanza?
o: A group of lines in a poem
A kind of actor on a stage
A chapter of a book, usually

questions.q: Which text is prose?
questions.why: Prose is in sentences and paragraphs.

questions.q: In a script, what do brackets like (laughs) usually show?
A text has short lines, rhyming ends, and four-line groups. What is it?
What does dialogue mean?
o: A long description of a place and its weather
A rhyme at the end of a line

questions.q: Match each form to a feature.
questions.why: Each form has its own layout.

questions.q: Why can a poem say a lot in few words?
o: Each word and image is chosen with care
Poets pick long words because they sound grand and clever
Poems use fewer ideas than stories

questions.q: Why does a script need stage directions as well as spoken words?
questions.model: Because the audience also sees what characters do, so the script tells actors how to move, where to stand and what the setting is, which are not in the spoken words.

questions.q: A story is retold as a play. What must be added?
o: Chapters of description with no speaking at all
questions.why: A play depends on speech and action.

panel.q: Why is a novel usually prose rather than a script?
o: It is meant to be read, with narration describing events
It is meant to be performed, so actors speak the lines aloud on a stage
Scripts are against the law to write
Prose has no words in it, only ideas

panel.q: A poem lacks rhyme but has strong rhythm and images. Is it still poetry?
o: No, because rhyme is always required
Only if it has a title

panel.q: Compare how a story event might be shown in prose and in a play.
panel.model: In prose a narrator describes the event and thoughts in paragraphs, while in a play the event is shown through speech and action on stage.

teach.model: Prose is ordinary writing in sentences. Poetry uses lines and stanzas with rhythm. Drama is a script made to be acted with dialogue. For example, a novel is prose and a play is drama.

stages.title: Plot and character development
stages.hook: Why do some stories feel exciting right in the middle and calm at the end?
explain: A plot is the chain of events in a story. A common shape has five parts: the exposition (we meet the characters and setting), the rising action (trouble grows), the climax (the most tense moment), the falling action (things calm) and the resolution (the end).
Characters are the heart of a plot. A character develops when they learn or change, for example a shy girl who finds courage. A writer shows character by what people say, do and think.
Conflict drives a plot. It can be person against person, person against nature, or a struggle inside a person.

example.q: Find the climax: Tomas is afraid of the high diving board. He climbs it slowly. He stands at the edge, takes a breath and jumps. He splashes and cheers.
steps: Exposition: Tomas is afraid.
Rising action: he climbs.
Climax: the moment he jumps.
Resolution: he cheers.

analogies.home: A game of hide and seek rises to the moment someone is found.
analogies.sport: A match builds up to a final goal, its climax.
analogies.nature: A storm builds, breaks, and fades.
analogies.music: A song can build to a loud peak and then soften.

stages.mnemonic: Plot is a hill: climb, top, slide down.
terms: The sequence of events in a story.
The most tense or important moment.
The struggle at the heart of a story.

misc.wrong: The climax is the end of the story.
misc.right: The climax is the peak of tension. The resolution comes after it.

trip.prompt: Find where the climax of a story is placed on the plot diagram.

questions.q: What is the climax of a story?
What is exposition?
o: The final scene, where every problem is settled

questions.q: A character who is selfish at the start but learns to share has...
A boy struggles against a flood. Which conflict?
questions.why: The flood is a force of nature.

questions.q: A girl cannot decide whether to tell the truth. Which conflict?
Order the parts of a plot.
questions.why: This is the usual five-part shape.

questions.q: How can a writer show a character is kind without saying so?
o: Name them Kind and leave it there

questions.q: Why does a story need a conflict?
questions.model: Without a conflict or problem nothing much would happen, so the conflict gives the story events, tension and a reason to read on.
questions.why: Conflict creates tension and drives the plot.

questions.q: A story jumps straight from the climax to "The end". What is missing?
o: The exposition at the very start
questions.why: The loose ends are not tied up.

questions.q: Which sentence best shows a character developing?
o: At first Ravi hid from the crowd, but by the end he proudly sang on stage.
Ravi wore a blue coat on his way to the concert hall every day, and he liked it.
Ravi lived in a house with a small garden behind it, near the bakery.
Ravi had lunch at noon, as he always did, and then he went home to rest.

panel.q: Why might a writer put the climax near the end?
A character never changes at all in a long story. What effect might that have?
o: It must really be a poem instead
The plot gets longer and longer

panel.q: Pick a story you know and explain its conflict and how it was resolved.
panel.model: In The Tortoise and the Hare the conflict is the race between a quick, careless hare and a steady tortoise; it is resolved when the tortoise crosses the line first.
panel.why: A good answer names the problem and its solution.

teach.model: A plot is the chain of events. It rises to a climax and then settles in a resolution. Conflict is the problem that drives it. Characters develop when they change or learn.

stages.title: Themes and messages
stages.hook: After a story ends, what idea stays in your head? That idea might be its theme.
explain: A theme is the big idea a story explores, such as friendship, courage, honesty or loss. A theme is not the same as the plot. The plot says what happens; the theme says what the story is really about.

A moral is a clear lesson, often stated at the end of a fable. A theme can be bigger and quieter. A story may not tell you the lesson. You work it out from what the characters do and what happens to them.
To find a theme, ask: What problem do the characters face? What do they learn? Then say it as an idea, not a story: not "a hare loses a race" but "careless pride can lead to failure".

example.q: Find the theme: Mei and Kofi disagree and stop speaking. Each misses the other. Mei says sorry first and they laugh again.
steps: Problem: a quarrel breaks a friendship.
What changes: someone says sorry.
Big idea: friendship can be repaired by forgiveness.

analogies.home: Many family tales are about sharing and caring.
analogies.city: A story about a lost wallet being returned may be about honesty.
analogies.sport: A team story could be about working together.
analogies.nature: A seed that grows in hard soil may be about hope.

stages.mnemonic: Theme = the big idea you take home in your pocket.
terms: The central idea or message explored by a story.
A lesson stated clearly, as in a fable.
What the author wants us to think about.

misc.wrong: The theme is just what happens in the story.
misc.right: The plot is what happens. The theme is the idea behind it.

stages.limits: Readers can find different themes in the same story, because stories have many layers.

trip.prompt: See how themes differ from plots.

questions.q: What is a theme?
o: The big idea of a story
The first line of the story
The list of all the characters
questions.why: A theme is the central idea.

questions.q: Which is a theme?
o: The story is in a village
questions.why: A theme is an idea, not an event.

questions.q: In a fable, the lesson written at the end is called...
A story shows a team that wins only when everyone helps. A good theme is...
questions.why: The events point to working together.

questions.q: How do we usually find a theme?
o: Count how many words are on each page of it
Look at the colour of the cover
questions.why: Characters' choices and lessons point to theme.

questions.q: The plot says "an ant stores food in summer and a grasshopper does not". The theme might be...
questions.why: Plot becomes theme when you state the idea.

questions.q: Match each story to a theme.
pairs: A boy returns a lost wallet
A weak mouse frees a lion
A shy girl sings at last
questions.why: Each story shows an idea in action.

questions.q: In your own words, what is the difference between the plot and the theme of a story?
questions.model: The plot is the series of events in the story, while the theme is the big idea behind them, such as courage or honesty.
questions.why: Plot is what happens; theme is what it means.

questions.q: Two readers find different themes in the same story. Why is that possible?
o: Stories can have several ideas, and readers notice different ones
One of the two readers is always wrong, whatever they say or feel
Stories hold no ideas in them

questions.q: Which statement is a theme, not a plot summary?
o: A king asks for gold and gets it.
The king goes to a river.

panel.q: Why do many cultures tell stories about kindness?
o: People everywhere value caring for others
Kindness is rare, so people tell tales about it
A law says so in every land
panel.why: Common values appear in stories worldwide.

panel.q: A story never states its lesson. How do you know the theme?
o: By thinking about events and choices
You cannot know it, so you must give up
By guessing from the title alone
By measuring how many pages there are

panel.q: Choose a story and give its theme in a sentence, with one reason from the story.
panel.model: In The Tortoise and the Hare the theme is that steady effort beats careless pride, because the hare naps and loses to the tortoise who keeps going.
panel.why: A theme is backed by an event.

teach.model: A theme is the big idea in a story, like honesty or courage. The plot is what happens. The theme is what it means. You find it by asking what the characters learn.

points.ask: How is it different from plot?

stages.title: Basic poetic devices
stages.hook: "The moon is a silver coin." Is the moon really a coin? Why would a poet say that?
explain: Poets use devices to make words vivid. A simile compares two things using like or as: "as quick as a fox". A metaphor says one thing is another: "the moon is a silver coin".

Alliteration repeats the starting sound in nearby words: "sally sells seashells". Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like what it names: buzz, splash, crash. Personification gives human actions to things: "the wind whispered".
Rhyme matches end sounds. Rhythm is the beat made by strong and soft syllables. Repetition repeats words or lines for effect. These devices help us see, hear and feel the poem.

example.q: Spot the device: "The sun smiled down on the sleepy town."
steps: The sun cannot really smile.
A human action is given to a thing.
That is personification.

analogies.home: "Cold as ice" is a simile from the freezer.
analogies.city: Traffic honk and screech are onomatopoeia.
analogies.nature: "The stream chattered" gives water a voice.

stages.mnemonic: Simile says LIKE, metaphor says IS; alliteration repeats the start, onomatopoeia is a sound-word.
terms: A comparison using like or as.
Saying one thing is another to make a picture.
Repeated starting sounds in nearby words.
A word that imitates a sound.
Giving human actions to non-human things.

misc.wrong: A metaphor must use the word like.
misc.right: Like and as belong to similes. A metaphor says directly that one thing is another.

trip.prompt: Find examples of similes and metaphors.

questions.q: "Her smile was as bright as the sun" is...
"The classroom was a zoo" is...
questions.why: It says one thing is another.

questions.q: Which is onomatopoeia?
"Peter picked purple plums" shows...
"The wind whispered through the trees" is...
Why do poets use similes?
o: To help readers see something in a fresh way
To make poems shorter and much quicker to read aloud

questions.q: Match the device to its example.
Explain how a simile and a metaphor are different.
questions.model: A simile compares two things using like or as, while a metaphor says one thing is another without using those words.
questions.why: The signal words are the difference.

questions.q: "The thunder growled angrily" uses...
o: Only a simile, using the word like
questions.why: Growling and anger are living things' actions.

questions.q: A poet repeats the line "Rain, rain, rain" at the end of each stanza. Why?
o: To make a rhythm and stress the feeling
To fill up the space so every stanza looks the same length

panel.q: If the moon is a "silver coin", what does the poet want you to notice?
o: That it is made of metal
panel.why: A metaphor highlights shared qualities, not literal truth.

panel.q: Why is "boom" a better word than "loud noise" in a poem about fireworks?
o: It is longer and it fills the page more
It is less clear to hear
panel.why: Onomatopoeia brings sound into the line.

panel.q: Make up a simile about the sea and explain what it describes.
panel.model: The sea was as calm as a sleeping cat, which shows it was quiet and still.
panel.why: A good simile names two things and a shared quality.

teach.model: Poets use devices to paint pictures. A simile compares with like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Alliteration repeats starting sounds, and onomatopoeia imitates sound.

stages.title: Introduction to theatre
stages.hook: If you wanted to put a story on stage, who would you need?
explain: Theatre is the art of telling a story by live performers in front of an audience. The play is written in a script. Actors play the characters, and a director guides the whole show.
Other helpers work backstage: designers make costumes and scenery, and stage crew move props, which are objects used on stage. The stage is the place where actors perform.
Theatre is very old. In ancient Greece people gathered in open-air theatres to watch plays. In Shakespeare's time in England, plays were shown in theatres such as the Globe, which opened in 1599.

example.q: Plan a tiny play: The Hare and the Tortoise.
steps: Cast: choose actors for hare and tortoise.
Make costumes (long ears, a shell) and a finish-line prop.
The director shows where to stand and run.
example.a: You need actors, costumes, props, a stage and a director.

analogies.home: Children playing pretend at home are doing a kind of theatre.
analogies.city: A city theatre has a stage, seats and lights.
analogies.sport: A team and coach work like actors and director.
analogies.music: An orchestra and a conductor are like actors and a director.

stages.mnemonic: Script, Actors, Director, Props, Stage: SADPS, a show begins.
terms: The written words and directions of a play.
The person who guides how the play is staged.
An object used by actors on stage.

misc.wrong: Actors make up every word as they go.
misc.right: Most plays follow a written script that actors learn and rehearse.

trip.prompt: Find the jobs people do to make a play happen.

questions.q: Who guides how a play is staged?
What is a prop?
o: A seat for the audience in the hall
questions.why: Props are things like a sword or a cup.

questions.q: Where do actors learn their words and movements?
questions.why: The script has the words and directions.

questions.q: The Globe Theatre was linked with which writer?
questions.why: Shakespeare's company performed at the Globe.

questions.q: A play needs a king's crown. Who might make it?
o: The audience, sitting in the stalls
The ticket seller at the door
questions.why: Designers and crew make such things.

questions.q: In which country did people watch plays in open-air theatres long ago?
Put the steps of making a play in order.
questions.why: A script comes first, then practice, then the show.

questions.q: Match the job to its task.
Why does a play need rehearsals before the audience comes?
questions.model: Actors need to learn their lines and movements and work together, so the show runs smoothly and confidently for the audience.

questions.q: Why is live theatre different from a film?
o: The audience and actors share the same space and moment
The film is shot in one take, while theatre is made of many cuts
It has no story, only noise

panel.q: Why might a theatre use few props on a bare stage?
o: Words and imagination can create the setting
Props are forbidden by the law of the land, so the stage stays bare

panel.q: In Shakespeare's day, scenery was simple. What did the words do?
o: Helped paint the place in the audience's mind
Nothing at all, because the scenery did all of the work for them
panel.why: Poetic descriptions told where we were.

panel.q: Explain why a play is a team effort, not just the work of the writer.
panel.model: A play is brought to life by many people, including actors, a director, designers and crew, who all work together to turn the script into a show.

teach.model: Theatre is a story performed live on a stage. A script gives the words. Actors play characters and a director guides them. Costumes and props help the audience believe the place.

stages.title: African folktales
stages.hook: The same small clever trickster appears in tales from different lands. What might make a trickster so loved?
explain: Africa has thousands of storytelling traditions. Anansi the spider comes from the Akan people of Ghana. In many tales he uses cleverness to outwit bigger creatures, and he also sometimes gets caught by his own tricks.

The Yoruba people of Nigeria tell tales of Ijapa the tortoise, a trickster whose wits make up for his small size. Amazigh (Berber) peoples of North Africa tell tales that reflect desert, mountain and village life.

The Epic of Sundiata is a West African story of Sundiata Keita, the founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century. Griots, who are traditional West African oral historians and musicians, have kept the epic alive by telling and singing it for many generations.

example.q: Who tells and keeps the Sundiata story?
steps: The epic is long and old.
Griots in West Africa tell it with music.
They pass it from teacher to student.
example.a: Griots, through spoken and sung performance.

analogies.home: Elders tell Anansi stories in the evening to children.
analogies.music: Griots accompany stories with instruments such as the kora.

stages.mnemonic: Anansi the spider spins a tale; the griot sings the king.
terms: A clever spider trickster in Akan tales from Ghana.
A West African oral historian and musician.
A clever character who uses wit, often to break rules.
A long story about heroes and great events.

misc.wrong: All African tales are the same.
misc.right: Africa has many peoples and languages, each with its own stories, characters and traditions.

stages.limits: Tellers vary tales, so there is no single correct version.

trip.prompt: Look for what makes Anansi a trickster.

questions.q: Which people first told Anansi stories?
o: The Inuit of the far north

questions.q: Who is Ijapa in Yoruba tales?
o: A king of the Yoruba, long ago

questions.q: What is a griot?
o: A West African oral historian and musician
A kind of tall spider that lives in the forest of West Africa

questions.q: The Epic of Sundiata is about the founder of which empire?
questions.why: Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire.

questions.q: A small trickster beats a big animal using wit in a tale. What does that show about the tale's message?
o: Strength always matters most and wit is useless
Small things must fear the big

questions.q: Why do tales often name the people they come from?
o: To honour the community that kept them
To make them shorter and easier to say

questions.q: Match the tale or tradition to its people.
questions.why: These are three traditions of West Africa.

questions.q: Why does a griot use music?
o: It helps memory and makes the story powerful
It is required by law in every village, so a griot must sing

questions.q: Why do you think trickster tales are loved in many communities?
questions.model: They are fun and funny, and they show that a small or weak character can win by being clever, while also teaching lessons about the results of tricks.
questions.why: Humour and wit make tricksters popular.

questions.q: Order how an epic like Sundiata can survive without writing.
items: A griot learns the story from a teacher
The griot performs it with music
Listeners remember it and tell others
The tale is kept for the next generation
questions.why: Oral tradition passes tales from person to person.

panel.q: Why can there be many versions of an Anansi tale?
o: Each teller adds their own details when telling
Anansi is not a real spider, so anyone can say anything they like
It is always printed in the same way

panel.q: A trickster tale ends with Anansi caught by his own trick. What might it teach?
o: Spiders are slow, so they are caught
Tricks always win in the end

panel.q: Explain why it is better to say "Akan tales from Ghana" than just "African tales".
panel.model: Africa has many peoples and cultures, so naming the Akan of Ghana is accurate and gives credit to the community the tale comes from.

teach.model: Anansi is a spider trickster from the Akan people of Ghana. The Yoruba of Nigeria tell of Ijapa the tortoise. Griots in West Africa keep the Epic of Sundiata by telling and singing it.

stages.title: European and Asian folktales
stages.hook: Tales travel on ships, caravans and tongues. Which tales do you think crossed the world?
explain: Europe: Aesop's fables come from ancient Greece. The Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm, collected German folktales and published them from 1812. Norse mythology from Scandinavia tells of gods such as Thor and Odin. Arthurian legends tell of King Arthur and his knights.
India: the Panchatantra is a collection of animal fables in Sanskrit that teaches wise living. Jataka tales are stories about the Buddha's earlier lives, often told with animals.

The One Thousand and One Nights is a collection of tales from the Middle East and South Asia, framed by Scheherazade telling stories to the king. In Japan the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy, is well loved. In China, Journey to the West follows the monk Xuanzang and the Monkey King Sun Wukong.

example.q: Find where the tale comes from: the Monkey King.
steps: Monkey King is Sun Wukong.
He appears in Journey to the West.
That is a Chinese novel from the 16th century.

analogies.home: Grandparents tell Grimm tales at bedtime in many countries.
analogies.city: Bookshops stock tales from many lands.
analogies.music: Tale songs and ballads help tales travel.

stages.mnemonic: Greece, Germany, India, Arabia, Japan, China: tales on a world tour.
terms: A magical story, often with a hero and a happy ending.
Stories of the Buddha's past lives.
A story that holds other stories inside it.

misc.wrong: Fairy tales were invented by one writer.
misc.right: Most were told by many people over time and later collected by writers.

stages.limits: The Grimms edited the tales they collected, so printed versions are not exactly the tellers' words.

trip.prompt: Find the tales the Grimms collected and which ones you know.

questions.q: Who collected German folktales in books from 1812?
The Panchatantra is a collection of...
o: Greek plays from the ancient stage
Poems about the sea and ships
Maps of the old kingdoms and roads
questions.why: It teaches wisdom with animal tales.

questions.q: Who tells the stories in One Thousand and One Nights?
o: Aesop, the old Greek fable teller
questions.why: She is the storyteller in the frame story.

questions.q: Who is Momotaro?
o: A hero born from a peach in a Japanese tale
A Greek god who rules over the sea and storms
A German king in the Black Forest

questions.q: Which tradition tells of Thor and Odin?
Why might the same tale appear in several countries with small changes?
o: Travellers carry tales and tellers adapt them
Tales cannot move from place to place at all, so it must be chance
Authors must copy them by law

questions.q: Match the tale to its land.
questions.why: Each comes from a different region.

questions.q: Scheherazade keeps telling tales that stop at an exciting moment. Why?
o: To make the king want to hear the next one
Because she forgot the rest of the story and had to stop
questions.why: It is a frame story of suspense.

questions.q: Why do animals appear so often in fables from Greece and India?
questions.model: Animals can stand for human habits, so fables can teach lessons about people in a simple and gentle way.

questions.q: Order the journey of a tale to a modern child.
items: People tell the tale by mouth
It is printed in a book
questions.why: Many tales were first oral and written later.

panel.q: Why must we remember the Grimms edited their tales?
o: Printed versions differ from what tellers said
They invented every one of the tales themselves
They never met anyone who knew a tale
They wrote them all in a secret code

panel.q: A frame story holds other stories inside it. Which fits?
o: The One Thousand and One Nights
A single fable with one clear moral
panel.why: Scheherazade's tales are inside the frame.

panel.q: Explain how one fable from the Panchatantra and one from Aesop can teach similar ideas though they come from different lands.
panel.model: People in many places face similar problems and value similar things, such as wisdom and caution, so fables from different lands can share lessons.

teach.model: Aesop's fables come from Greece and the Grimms collected German tales. In India the Panchatantra uses animals to teach. The Nights has Scheherazade telling stories. Japan has Momotaro and China has the Monkey King.

stages.title: Indigenous American and Oceanian folktales
stages.hook: How can a hero fish up an island or slow down the sun? Which people tell such tales?
explain: Indigenous peoples of the Americas and Oceania have rich story traditions. Many are shared openly, and some are kept for particular people. We learn from those shared publicly, and we name the peoples they come from.

In Polynesia, the demigod Māui is a famous hero. In Māori tradition he fished up the North Island of New Zealand, called Te Ika-a-Māui, the fish of Māui. In Hawaiian tradition he is said to have slowed the sun so that days would be longer.

The K'iche' Maya book Popol Vuh tells that the first people were made from maize. The Inuit of the Arctic have many stories shared on long winter nights. The Mapuche, Guaraní and many Brazilian peoples have tales of forest spirits. Aboriginal Australian storytelling, often called Dreaming stories, explains the land and living things; some are for everyone to hear and some are restricted.

example.q: Say where Māui's fish tale comes from.
steps: The island is Te Ika-a-Māui.
It is the North Island of New Zealand.
The people are the Māori.
example.a: The Māori people of Aotearoa New Zealand.

analogies.home: Elders pass tales to children at home.
analogies.sea: Polynesian voyagers told tales of the ocean and islands.
analogies.nature: Many tales explain mountains, rivers and animals.

stages.mnemonic: Maui fishes, maize makes people, Dreaming shapes land: three tales, three peoples.
terms: A Polynesian hero who in Māori tale fished up the North Island.
A K'iche' Maya book of creation stories.
Aboriginal Australian stories and law about the land.
First or original peoples of a place.

misc.wrong: All Indigenous stories can be retold by anyone.
misc.right: Some stories are sacred or restricted and belong to certain people. We use only those shared openly and credit the community.

stages.limits: Names, spellings and versions differ between peoples and tellers.

trip.prompt: Find the different adventures of Māui.

questions.q: Which people tell of Māui fishing up the North Island?
In the Popol Vuh, what were the first people made from?
questions.why: The K'iche' Maya tell of people made from maize.

questions.q: What are Dreaming stories?
o: Aboriginal Australian stories about land and life
Fairy tales from the forests and castles of Germany
questions.why: They explain the land and law.

questions.q: Why do we not tell restricted stories?
o: They are for particular people and must be respected
They are boring, so nobody wants to tell them any more
questions.why: Respect for who may hear them.

questions.q: In Hawaiian tradition, what did Māui do to the sun?
o: Slowed it so days were longer
Painted it a new colour with a brush

questions.q: Match the story to its people.
questions.why: Each is told by different peoples.

questions.q: A book says "Native American tale" with no tribe named. What would be better?
o: Name the specific nation it comes from
Say nothing about where it came from, so as not to offend
Call it a fairy tale instead
questions.why: There are many nations with different stories.

questions.q: Why do many stories from island peoples feature the sea and fishing?
questions.model: These peoples lived on or near the sea and depended on it for food and travel, so their stories reflect the ocean and fishing.

questions.q: Order the steps of respectful retelling.
items: Find a story shared openly by the community
Name the people it comes from

questions.q: Why might a tale about a forest spirit be told to children in the Amazon?
o: To teach care and respect for the forest
To sell things in the market there
To scare them just for fun, nothing more

panel.q: Why is it important to credit each people by name?
o: It honours them and avoids mixing up cultures
It makes stories longer and more fun to read aloud
It is a rule for poems
panel.why: Each people has its own tradition.

panel.q: What does it mean that some Dreaming stories are restricted?
o: Only certain people may hear or tell them
They are lost and nobody can find them any more
panel.why: Knowledge can be held with responsibility.

panel.q: Explain why a tale about Māui cannot be treated as the same as a tale from the Popol Vuh.
panel.model: They come from different peoples and cultures with their own beliefs and places, so each tale has its own meaning and should be understood on its own terms.

teach.model: The Māori tell of Māui fishing up the North Island. The K'iche' Maya tell of people made from maize in the Popol Vuh. Aboriginal Australians share Dreaming stories. Some stories are restricted, so we use only those shared openly.
